To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the English city riots and the responses to it bear a remarkable resemblance in terms of the moral panic that it caused and the way it was framed in terms of “moral decline” and “lack of self restraint” among certain sections.

(1) the responses to the English City Riots 2011 bear remarkable similarities to those of historical disorders, (2) the retreat into the present is evident among both the policy discourse and the social science in responding contemporary urban disorder, (3) the previous moral panics have been focused on young and working class population and urban disorder, (4) the previous techniques of governance were often more similar to contemporary ones than many commentaries suggested.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the way in which the present is framed by a sense of crisis and moral decline, and how the past is used to inform this.

the historical and social scientific study of urban disorder, and the way in which it is framed by concerns over moral decline, social malaise and a lack of self-restraint among certain sections of urban populations.
the way in which the English riots of 2010/2011 have been framed and interpreted in relation to the historical record.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there has been a retreat into the present in the responses to urban disorder and the English city riots, and that a long-term, historical analysis can provide the necessary perspective to understand the present.
, while there may be no ‘Broken Britain’, there is certainly a ‘Broken Britain’ narrative.
the current concerns over urban disorder and anti- social behaviour are not unique, and are not a product of the present time, but are in fact a common feature of the urban condition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are not living in the most ‘broken’ of times; rather we are simply experiencing the latest iteration of a long-standing moral panic.
the English city riots were a product of the urban condition and not a product of the current era.
the English city riots and their aftermath have been framed by a retreat into the present and the re-imagining of a golden age of civility.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a more ‘detached’ perspective is required to appreciate that perceived “crises” of civilisation are not new to the urban condition.
the English city riots and their aftermath are not unique to the present, but rather a continuation of a long-standing tradition of urban disorder and the responses to it.

a historical perspective is vital for the study of contemporary social issues, and that a detached, long-term perspective is essential for the study of the urban disorder and the governance of young people in particular.
